newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Buba urges Bonn to pass savings plan for EMU.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Buba urges Bonn to pass savings plan for EMU.

text.p: The Bundesbank on Thursday urged parliament to approve Chancellor Helmut Kohl's austerity plan, saying the measures had to be implemented in full to allow Germany to qualify for European monetary union.

The central bank said the planned cuts could push Germany's deficit down to the required three percent of Gross Domestic Product or below in 1997, the year for deciding which countries can join in the scheduled 1999 launch of the single currency.

"It is urgently necessary for the budget relief planned by the government to be realised in its total volume. States and local municipalities must also contribute," the German central bank said in its September monthly report.

"If this is successful, and the economy continues to improve, the state deficit could fall to three percent of GDP or a little below so Germany would fulfil deficit criteria for entry into currency union in the decisive 1997 year," it said.
The three percent deficit-to-GDP rate is one of several strict criteria for membership of the single currency laid down in the Maastricht Treaty on European Union.

The report was released ahead of Friday's expected vote in the German lower house of parliament on Kohl's plan to push through spending cuts totalling 70 billion marks ($46 billion) next year to whip Bonn's finances in shape.
The package aims to slash 50 billion marks from public spending and 20 billion marks from social welfare fund spending next year in a bid to meet Maastricht Treaty requirements.
But the Bundesbank said it could not rule out that the nation's budget deficit may rise to four percent of GDP this year after totalling 3.5 percent of GDP last year.
The German central bank also warned that the government's debt could rise above 60 percent of the country's GDP, another Maastricht Treaty requirement.

Initial membership in the European currency, slated to begin in January 1999, should be decided in early 1998, making 1997 data crucial to the debate over which countries will take part in the launch.
The report also said the nation's total deficit, including federal, state and local debt, rose in the second quarter to 23.5 billion marks from 16.5 billion in the year-ago period.
The Bundesbank blamed a slowdown in the development of tax inflows and the weak economy, coupled with changes in German tax laws, for the higher deficit.
The Bundesbank also sounded a cautious note on Germany's outlook, saying it was unclear whether the economy had overcome its weakness despite a second-quarter return to buoyant growth.

The report said the economic situation appeared to be improving in several important sectors and, echoing government officials, predicted full-year GDP growth could slightly exceed an earlier government forecast of 0.75 percent.

But a 1.5 percent rise in real second-quarter GDP from the first three months overstated the upturn because it was partly fuelled by a resurgence in construction activity after the end of a long, cold winter.
"Whether this means the economic weakness which started in the second half of 1995 has already been finally overcome remains to be seen," the Bundesbank said.
The rise in building activity accounted for about a third of growth in the second quarter, the bank said, noting that inflation was not a danger.
Structural problems also persisted in the economy, which the Bundesbank said would be "at best be covered over if the economic upturn continues."
GDP growth was being driven mainly by an increase in foreign demand since the start of 1996 as economic growth in other major countries fuelled exports of industrial goods.
